description_full: Dino Polska S.A., together with its subsidiaries, operates a network of medium-sized grocery supermarkets under the Dino brand in Poland. The company stores offer fresh food products, such as meat, poultry, cold cuts, fruits and vegetables, dairy products, and bread; other groceries, including children's food, breakfast products, ready to eat meals, beverages, candies, snacks, frozen goods, processed goods, oils, grain and bulk products, condiments, and alcohol and cigarettes; and non-grocery products comprising flowers, cleaning agents, sanitary articles, pet food, seasonal products, and small household appliances. It also produces meat products; rents and operates owned and leased real estate; purchases and sells real estate properties; and manufactures and processes refined petroleum products, as well as offers other financial services. In addition, it engages in the retail sale of automotive fuel in specialized stores; operation of warehousing and storage facilities; retail sales run by mail order houses or the internet; and advertising agency activities. The company was founded in 1999 and is based in Krotoszyn, Poland.

financial_summary: DINO POLSKA SA is a mid-cap consumer defensive business with a $9.4B market cap on $8.4B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +26% over the past three years, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder.

Returns on capital run at 25% against a 7% cost of capital — a 18-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat, and 23% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.

The business throws off $153M in free cash flow — roughly 2 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.73× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage of 17× is fortress-like.
Shareholder yield is only 0.0%, a thin return of capital, and insiders hold 51% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is.
